etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin resolutus (“released”), past participle of resolvō (“I release, I unbind”).

quote.citation: c. 1591–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Third Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iv]:
quote.text: Edward is at hand, / Ready to fight; therefore be resolute.

quote.citation: a. 1887 (date written), Emily Dickinson, “I'm the little “Heart's Ease”!”, in Martha Dickinson Bianchi and Alfred Leete Hampson, editors, Further Poems of Emily Dickinson, Boston, Mass.: Little, Brown, and Company, published 1929, page 69:
quote.text: If the Coward Bumble Bee / In his chimney corner stay, / I, must resoluter be!

quote.citation: 2011 April 10, Alistair Magowan, “Aston Villa 1 - 0 Newcastle”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: Villa had plenty of opportunities to make the game safe after a shaky start and despite not reaching any great heights, they were resolute enough to take control of the game in the second half.

definitions.definition: A determined person; one showing resolution.
(mathematics) A projection onto an arbitrary vector.
